finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> performs no authorization check: require_allowed (is_allowed) returns a bool whose result is discarded, so any caller can delete any stored file.
finding.source: views.py:15-16 DELETE /files/<fid> (any client, fid from URL path)

trace.note: DELETE route defined, no per-route auth beyond before_request
load_user sets g.user from header for all requests
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') called; return value (bool) ignored
is_allowed returns a bool, does not raise

finding.guards_checked: before_request sets g.user but does not enforce; is_allowed result unused at views.py:18; compare rename_file at views.py:26 which uses ensure_allowed (aborts 403) correctly

verdict.guard_found: none effective. views.py:10-12 (load_user) only copies the X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user and enforces nothing. views.py:18 calls require_allowed, which is the alias of acl.py:4 is_allowed (a bool-returning function that never raises), as a bare statement, so its result is discarded. views.py:19 then runs del STORE[fid] unconditionally. The correct pattern is used only on the rename route at views.py:26 (ensure_allowed, which calls abort(403) at acl.py:10).
verdict.reason: The DELETE route at views.py:15-19 deletes STORE[fid] at line 19 regardless of the result of require_allowed at line 18, which is the aliased is_allowed (acl.py:4) returning a bool that is never tested, so any caller who can reach the endpoint can delete any file. The attacker needs no role at all, since the only check is a client-supplied header with no enforcement. The trace matches the code line for line.

finding.claim: Caller identity is taken directly from the X-Session-User-Verified request header with no signature, session, or trusted-proxy verification in this code, so authorization decisions can be spoofed if the header is not stripped and set upstream.
finding.sink: views.py:18 and views.py:26 grant checks via g.user

trace.note: before_request load_user applies to all routes
